title: Sticking to Safe Topics Can Keep Us Stuck on the Wrong Side of Science
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Reading specialist Harriett Janetos responds to whole language professor Andy Johnson, who agreed to discuss word recognition and word identification but declined to engage with how word confirmation fits within the three-cueing system. Janetos argues that the three-cueing system can and must be taught, provided the distinction is kept clear: graphemes and phonemes do the work of identifying a word, while syntax and semantics confirm it. Her key move is to separate what proficient readers do simultaneously from how beginners should be taught, comparing it to a basketball player who learns component skills before integrating them. She grounds the argument in classroom examples of first graders flexing vowel sounds until a decoded word makes sense, and cites a 2026 review by Nicholas and Bradbury that describes this self-monitoring process. Janetos also rebuts Johnson's claim that phonics is inefficient for working memory by invoking George Miller's work on chunking and Linnea Ehri's orthographic mapping, and rejects the idea that teachers should teach all six types of phonics named by the National Reading Panel. The essay closes by criticizing ridicule in place of research-based debate and by calling struggling readers casualties of a systemic, not teacher, failure.
points: Janetos distinguishes word identification (decoding graphemes and phonemes) from word confirmation (checking syntax and semantics), arguing that state bans targeted the undifferentiated cueing model.
She argues that the brain's simultaneous use of language systems in skilled reading does not mean beginners should be taught to use them simultaneously.
Using pictures or context to guess a word, rather than to confirm a decoding attempt, is said to bypass orthographic mapping and stall word recognition.
Miller's research on chunking is used to counter the claim that phonics overloads working memory, since readers quickly process graphemes, rimes and morphemes as units.
Telling teachers to use all six NRP phonics types is dismissed as offering a taxonomy rather than a pedagogy.
quotes: The brain's simultaneous utilization of three interactive and interdependent language systems (syntactic, semantic, and phonetic) during reading does not establish that these systems must be taught simultaneously.
Just coming up with a word based on pictures or context—rather than using context to confirm her decoding effort—bypasses the opportunity for orthographic mapping and can stall word recognition.

Of course, what is being banned is the original, undifferentiated system where the crucial distinction between identification and confirmation was never emphasized—the very point I wanted to discuss with Dr. Johnson.
Readers begin chunking letters into graphemes, rimes, and morphemes, none of which places a memory burden on the normally-developing reader.
But telling a teacher they have to teach all six types of phonics isn’t helpful because it just gives them a taxonomy, not a pedagogy.

Once again, compounding confusion: We are tinkering with lessons, not students. We are interested in effective and efficient teaching to maximize time available for reading and writing, and that’s why teaching necessitates tinkering.

This isn’t a failure on the part of their teachers. It’s a failure on the part of the larger system: misguided professors in education departments; uninformed district leaders; lack of meaningful professional development.
